For 2027, the immunosuppressive drug premium is $125.70.14:Tc2f,In this interim final rule (IFR), the Department of Commerce is establishing new rules to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on U.S. technology to threaten U.S. national security and foreign policy interests. First, this rule establishes new restrictions which will apply for exports, reexports, or transfers (in-country) to overseas data centers that remotely supply significant volumes of compute to companies headquartered in Country Group D:5 or Macau. These restrictions will undermine the ability of companies headquartered in countries of concern from using U.S. advanced Super Intelligence (SI) semiconductors to train advanced SI models. Data centers, foreign foundries, and chip exporters are required to perform robust due diligence on their customers, including any direct or indirect ownership or control by persons in Country Group D:5 or Macau, as part of complying with this new control. The license requirement will not apply to commercial recommender systems, such as those used by online retailers or social media companies, as these functions do not pose the same national security threat. Second, in addition to the current license requirements for advanced semiconductors, a license will be required to export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil (and any additional country designated by the Secretary of Commerce, in consultation with the Secretary of State or the Assistant to the President for National Security Affairs)--countries which present a higher-than-normal risk of diversion. The license requirement for these five countries will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in, or whose ultimate parent company is headquartered in, the United States, provided certain reporting requirements are met. Commerce will be actively monitoring for countries that tolerate evasion of this IFR and will consider a range of consequences for such countries, such as import restrictions, new license requirements on advanced semiconductor exports, downgrading the country's status in the U.S. export control regime, and Entity List designations and temporary export prohibitions for foreign persons involved in such activities. Third, this IFR amends the presumptions which front-end chips fabricators and chip packagers face when exporting advanced-node logic chips. These amendments reduce the number of pathways to overcome the presumptions for chip designers located in destinations which face a license requirement for SI chips. This change gives the U.S. government critical oversight over companies headquartered in certain countries that seek to leverage advanced semiconductor production capabilities in third countries. Finally, the IFR formally rescinds the regulations implementing the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The AI Diffusion Rule has never been enforced. Astronomers use those readings along with optical and infrared images from other NASA instruments to track the earliest stages of stellar development across the Milky Way and in nearby galaxies.

Four new sonifications released by the Chandra team turn those combined observations into sound. In the Messier 82 starburst galaxy the scan begins with a radar sweep that grows louder at brighter sources while X-rays occupy the highest frequencies and infrared appears as low drones and plucked notes. For the Orion Nebula more than a thousand infant stars register as twinkling sounds against a backdrop of pure high tones from diffuse X-ray emission and lower distorted strings from James Webb Space Telescope infrared data. The Carina Nebula’s Cosmic Cliffs region maps individual baby stars to short string bursts and the surrounding X-ray glow to longer sustained notes while Webb’s infrared view becomes a continuous tone interrupted by other instruments at ridges and stars. Read Ambassador Greer's full letter to the Wall Street Journal below. In his op-ed “How Do You Like Those Tariffs Now?” (Nov. 11), David Hebert asserts that economists’ predictions about tariffs came true: “Americans would pay them, trading partners would retaliate, and bullying our allies would backfire.” The data tell a different story on each of these points. The first point—that American consumers bore the brunt of the tariffs—doesn’t hold up to scrutiny. Caroline Freund of the University of California San Diego published a paper in July concluding that foreign exporters absorbed roughly 40% to 50% of the 2025 U.S. tariff increases through lower export prices, “much more than earlier studies suggested.” Importers of record, typically companies, covered much of the rest. Preston Caldwell, chief U.S. economist at Morningstar, told the Journal last year that “U.S. firms are still footing most of the tariff bill, having yet to pass more than a fraction of the tariff cost on to consumers.” Nor did the tariffs trigger sweeping global retaliation. While the Trump administration put tariffs on countries all around the world, only two attempted direct retaliation: China and Canada. But in both cases, these countries eventually rolled back some of their retaliatory measures while the U.S. maintained most of its new tariffs. China has resumed buying U.S. soybeans, easing China’s leverage over U.S. farmers. As for Mr. Hebert’s argument about “backfiring,” 19 U.S. trading partners, accounting for nearly 40% of global gross domestic product, signed deals with us. In these agreements, the U.S. agreed to impose a lower tariff rate in exchange for our trading partners’ resolution of longstanding tariff and nontariff barriers—a prize free-trade fundamentalists have sought for decades. But don’t take our word for it; workers, farmers and industry leaders have praised President Trump’s deals that open foreign markets while expanding domestic jobs and investment. The U.S. has exported over $300 billion in goods and services every month this year, breaking records. We are in the tenth month of a manufacturing expansion. The economy is close to full employment. While Europe’s economic growth is sluggish and Canada’s unemployment rate rose to 6.7% in October, the U.S. is the most dynamic economy in the Group of Seven. So, yes, we like these tariffs very much. ###22:T1e3a,Caring for nature is part of who we are as Canadians. As we build a stronger, more sustainable economy, Canada is taking ambitious action to protect the ecosystems that sustain our communities, our livelihoods, and our prosperity. Earlier this year, Canada’s government launched A Force of Nature , a historic $3.8 billion strategy to protect Canada’s natural environment, and announced a further $1.2 billion to safeguard our oceans and the life they sustain. In the Spring Economic Update 2026 , the government also committed to deliver nearly $6 billion in funding to support international climate finance, bringing Canada’s goal for climate finance to developing countries to over $13 billion by 2031. With these investments, Canada is strengthening its international partnerships and mobilising new capital to advance conservation beyond our borders and safeguard our planet for future generations. Today, the Prime Minister, Mark Carney, met with the President of Brazil, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, on the margins of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit in Manila, Philippines, where he announced an initial contribution of up to $560 million over four years to the Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF). Co-led by Brazil and Norway, this innovative financing mechanism is mobilising public and private investment to protect tropical forests, preserve biodiversity, and support the communities that depend on these vital ecosystems. Once fully operational, the TFFF will protect more than one billion hectares of tropical forests annually across more than 70 countries , with conservation payments tied to verified results. At least 20% of these payments will be directed to Indigenous Peoples and local communities, recognising their essential role in protecting forests and biodiversity. This pioneering model will also help shape new approaches to financing other global environmental and development priorities. Canada’s initial contribution will help meet the TFFF’s fundraising targets in order to launch operations and mobilise further public and private investment. This contribution is part of Canada’s goal, announced in the 2026 Spring Economic Update, to deliver over $13 billion in climate-related support to developing countries by 2031. Because the TFFF’s financial viability will depend on sustained support, Canada will also work with partners to broaden participation and deliver on the Facility’s objectives. Protecting tropical forests is essential to a stable climate, healthy ecosystems, and a resilient global economy. Their conservation benefits countries around the world, including Canada, where the impacts of climate change threaten communities, infrastructure, and economic prosperity. By mobilising new investment in nature and strengthening its partnership with Brazil, Norway, and other TFFF partners, Canada is helping safeguard vital ecosystems, reduce climate risks, and build a more sustainable and prosperous future for generations to come. To date, the TFFF has attracted growing international support, including financial commitments from Brazil, France, Germany, Indonesia, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, and the United Kingdom, as well as engagement from countries such as the Democratic Republic of Congo, Ghana, and Peru. The Facility aims to mobilise $35 billion in contributions from sponsoring countries and organisations to attract up to $140 billion in additional private investment. Net investment returns will fund long-term, performance-based conservation payments to eligible tropical forest countries.
